The basic idea behind Higgs inflation is that, in the very early universe, the Higgs field could have been strongly coupled to gravity, allowing it to influence the expansion of the universe. As the universe expanded and cooled, the Higgs field could have undergone a phase transition, causing it to become "metastable". This means that it would have a lower energy state than the surrounding universe, causing it to inflate at a faster rate than the rest of the universe.

This process is thought to have caused the universe to expand at an exponential rate, leading to the smooth and homogeneous universe that we observe today. The theory of Higgs inflation is still a topic of active research and debate in the physics community, and there is much that is still unknown about it. However, it has the potential to shed light on some of the biggest questions in physics, such as the nature of dark matter and dark energy, and the origin of the universe itself.
